proposition.object: A Stolen Dove Takes Flight Again

Outside a public library in Santa Ana, California, sat a bronze statue of a man with a book under one arm, a dove taking flight from the other. Palestinian-American poet, scholar, and civil rights leader Alex Odeh was assassinated in 1985; nine years later, Algerian-American artist Khalil Bendib made the statue in his honor. It was vandalized with red paint in 1996 and then again the year after; in 2020, the dove — a symbol of peace — was stolen, before eventually being recovered. Now, artist Jon Rubin is setting that dove free, sending it on a world tour as a living, participatory artwork that brings renewed attention to Odeh’s life and legacy, a continued history of anti-Arab violence, and efforts to end occupation and genocide in Palestine — a quiet prayer for peace. This past weekend, it flew to Los Angeles for an evening of music, poetry, and food; next, it’ll head to the Bay Area, Pittsburgh, and hopefully, to Jifna, Odeh’s hometown, before returning home to roost. It’s a timely reminder that art is something meant to be shared in community — as Patrick Guetta, the artist featured in this week’s edition of A View From the Easel, puts it, “One of my favorite museums is the street.” Also today, inside the cheerfully sinister worlds of Trevor Winkfield, and Zendaya wearing 3,000-year-old Iranian artifacts to a movie premiere points to bigger problems than out-of-touch celebrities. —Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor CORRECTION: Our Daily Newsletter from Friday, July 17, mistakenly stated that three antiquities the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office returned to Mexico were previously held at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, when in fact only one of them was.
